summary: This unit teaches you to handle the money side of a salon or spa accurately and honestly: prepare the till and the float, work out bills, take cash, card and other payments, give correct change and receipts, check notes, handle vouchers, deposits, discounts and refunds, keep cash safe, and cash up at the end of the day. You will also learn to give polite service at the till and to keep payment records correct and private.

blocks.p: Money is handled at the reception desk many times a day. A client who is charged correctly, given the right change and a receipt leaves happy; a client who is overcharged, shorted or kept waiting does not come back. For the salon, every dollar taken must be recorded, protected and accounted for at the end of the day. This unit is for COSMETOLOGY LEVEL 2 trainees, and it applies in a hair salon, a nail bar or a day spa.

Cashiers are trusted with the salon's money, so honesty and accuracy matter more than speed. A till that is a few dollars short is a warning that something is wrong, and an honest cashier reports it. Work every sum twice.

What this means in the salon

Add services and products correctly in J$
Apply a discount, a deposit or a voucher; add GCT at the rate given
Say the amount out loud; check the note; keep it on the counter
Count the change back into the client's hand
Chip and PIN, contactless, mobile and transfer; handle a declined card
Never record a card number or PIN
Give a receipt for every sale
Fill in the sales record correctly
Handle vouchers, deposits, discounts and refunds
Check a voucher is genuine, in date and unused
Record a deposit; get a supervisor's agreement for a refund or special discount
Close the drawer after each sale; lock or log out when leaving the desk
Take extra cash to the safe; vary bank trips
Cash up at the end of the day
Count and check the takings against the sales record

Give good service at the till
Greet, queue politely, explain the bill and deal with questions

blocks.h: A day at the payment point

flow: Prepare the till and float
Greet and bill the client

blocks.note: How you are assessed: theory papers (multiple-choice questions, short answers and essays, with sums in J$) and practical tasks in the Centre's reception: running a till with a float and several kinds of payment, and cashing up with a deposit slip. The assessor watches your accuracy, your honesty and your care with money and cards.

blocks.note: In practical work, use only the Centre's training money and practice slips. Never photograph real card numbers or clients' faces.

sections.title: Preparing the till and the payment point

blocks.p: A **float** is a set amount of change put in the till at the start of the day, in notes and coins of different values, so that the cashier can give correct change from the first sale. It is not the salon's takings.

flow: Collect the float from the safe, as the owner's procedure says
Count it with a supervisor or second person watching
Sort notes and coins by value
Write the amount on the float sheet and both sign it
Report any shortage or overage to the supervisor before taking sales
Place the money in the right sections of the drawer and close it

ul: **Why count it before opening?** To check it is the right amount before any sales are taken. A difference found at the end of the day cannot be traced to the float or to a sale.
**Why different values?** So the cashier can give clients the right change, for example a client paying with a large note for a small bill.
If the float is short, tell the supervisor and record the shortage before taking sales.

head: Check at the payment point
Why
rows: Till and card machine switch on and work; the machine is connected
Receipt rolls, pens, a calculator and a clean sales book
You cannot give a receipt without them.
Price list, offers list and appointment list at hand
Blank gift vouchers and refund forms
So you can issue and record them.
The counter is tidy; the drawer cannot be seen or reached by clients
In Jamaica the police are on 119.

blocks.note: Your own money does not go in the till. Keep your bag and phone in the staff area. If your own money is in the drawer, a difference at cash-up cannot be explained.
blocks.label: Remember

ul: Jamaica's currency is the Jamaican dollar (J$). The **Bank of Jamaica** issues the notes and coins.
Write money amounts clearly: J$1,250. Say amounts out loud: 'one thousand two hundred and fifty dollars.'
Learn the notes you handle every day so that you know them by sight and feel.

blocks.p: Add every service and product on the client's account, apply any discount, deposit or voucher, add GCT, and show her the total before she pays. Work it twice, or use the till's total and check it with a calculator.

head: Step
Example
rows: Wash and set J$4,200; hair product J$1,350
Add GCT at the rate you are given
The rate is whatever the salon tells you today; the till is usually set up to add it
Take off a deposit or voucher already paid
Deposit J$2,000 paid: balance to pay = total - J$2,000

head: Discount
Method
Worked example
rows: J$6,000: J$600 off; she pays J$5,400.
J$4,000: J$800 off; she pays J$3,200.
J$2,400: J$600 off; she pays J$1,800.

blocks.h: Worked bill with more than one item

blocks.p: A client has a manicure (J$2,500) and a pedicure (J$3,500), and buys a cuticle oil (J$1,200). The total before tax is J$2,500 + J$3,500 + J$1,200 = **J$7,200**. If she has a gift voucher worth J$8,000, the voucher covers the bill and the salon records the balance of the voucher.

blocks.note: General consumption tax (GCT) is added to most goods and services at the current rate set by law. Never use a rate from memory: use the rate the salon gives you or that the till is set to. Receipts show the tax separately.
blocks.label: Jamaica

blocks.note: Check each price against the price list, not from memory. A client who is overcharged by mistake loses trust; a client who is undercharged is a loss the salon must account for.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.h: Taking a cash payment and giving change

flow: Tell the client the total clearly
When she hands over money, say the amount out loud ('From five thousand')
Check the note's security features
Leave her note on the counter, not in the drawer, until she has her change
Key the amount into the till; it shows the change
Take out the change and count it back into her hand, starting from the amount of the bill
Put her note into the drawer and close it at once
Give her a receipt and thank her

ul: **Why keep her note on the counter?** So there is no argument about which note she gave you.
**Why count change back?** It lets the client see it is right, and starting from the bill amount, counting up, is the most reliable method.

blocks.p: **Counting change up:** for a J$2,600 bill paid with J$5,000, give J$400 and say 'three thousand', then J$2,000 and say 'five thousand', so she sees the total is J$5,000.
A **counterfeit** (forged) note is a fake made to look real. Check each larger note as you take it: look, feel and tilt.

head: Check
What to do
rows: Print and colours should be sharp and clear, with the security features the Bank of Jamaica describes for that note.
A real note has a feel you get to know, with raised print in places.
Features that change as the light moves.
With a note you know is real, if unsure.

blocks.p: If you think a note is forged, stay calm and polite and do not accuse the client; she may not know. Do not put it in the till or give it back to be passed on. Call the supervisor, who follows the salon's policy, which may include telling the police. Note what happened.

blocks.note: Keep the check discreet. Take the note, check it as you say the amount, and call your supervisor quietly. An accusation in front of other clients can lead to an argument.
blocks.label: Tip

head: Term
Meaning
rows: Point of sale machine: the card machine.
The client puts her card in the machine herself and keys in her PIN (personal identification number).
The client taps the card or phone on the machine to pay.
The machine will not approve the payment.

flow: Key the total into the card machine and show the client the amount
The client taps or inserts her own card
If a PIN is needed, she keys it in herself while you look away
Wait for the machine to show the payment is approved
Give her card back and her copy of the slip or receipt
Keep the salon's copy safely with the day's records

ul: **Never write down or keep a client's card number or PIN.** It can be used for fraud and it breaks her privacy.
Keep control of the machine; do not leave a card in it or the machine unattended.

If a card is **declined**, tell her quietly so others cannot hear, and do not suggest she has no money. You may try once more in case of a line fault, then politely ask if she has another way to pay. If there is a problem, call the supervisor.

head: Method
What to do
rows: An app or account on a phone that holds money. Wait for confirmation on the salon's machine or account before she leaves.
Check that the payment has reached the salon's account before she leaves; a screenshot is not proof.
Part cash and part card: take both and record each amount on the bill. Example: J$6,000 bill, she pays J$2,000 cash and J$4,000 card.
Only as the owner's policy allows; ask the supervisor.

blocks.note: Tips left on a card payment are recorded as tips, as the salon's policy says, and given to the staff member it was meant for. They are not part of the sales total.
blocks.label: Remember

sections.title: Receipts, vouchers, deposits, discounts and refunds

ul: Give a receipt for **every** sale, every time. It shows the **date, the items, the prices, any GCT and the total paid**.
Keep a copy or record of each receipt so the day's takings and the accounts can be checked.
A receipt is also the client's proof of purchase if she needs a refund or exchange.

flow: Check it is the salon's own voucher, with a number
Check it is in date and has not been used before, against the voucher record
Take its value off the bill; the client pays any extra
Mark it as used (or write the balance), with the date and number in the voucher record
Keep it with the day's takings for the cash-up

blocks.p: Example: a spa voucher worth J$8,000 and treatments that come to J$9,500: she pays the extra J$1,500.

A **deposit** is part of the price paid in advance to hold a booking, for example a bridal party or a spa day. Explain the amount and the cancellation policy before taking it. Take it by cash, card or transfer, give a receipt, and write the amount and receipt number on the booking. On the day, take the deposit off the total and the client pays the rest. Example: a bridal hair booking costs J$7,500; she paid J$2,000; J$5,500 is left to pay.

ul: Give only discounts that are on the salon's price list or offers list, for example a senior citizens' discount of 20% on a J$4,000 pedicure (she pays J$3,200).
A discount that is not on the list must be agreed by the manager or owner, following the salon's policy.

Never give a friend or relation a discount of your own. If a co-worker asks you to ring up her friend's service for less than the price list, refuse politely, and tell the supervisor if it happens again.

flow: Listen politely and apologise for the problem
Ask for the receipt, or look up the sale in the records
Look at the product to see if it is faulty, damaged or not as described
Check the salon's refund and exchange policy
Get the supervisor's agreement
Refund or exchange as the policy allows: card payments back onto the same card, cash in cash
Fill in the refund record: date, item, amount, reason and supervisor's signature; give a receipt for the refund

blocks.note: Refunds are recorded and signed by a supervisor to prevent mistakes and fraud and to keep the takings correct. Never refund from your own pocket or from the tip jar.
blocks.label: Safety

blocks.h: A client says she was charged twice

blocks.p: Listen, apologise, and check the bill against the sales record and the card slips. If she was overcharged, correct it as your supervisor agrees, and record it. Do not argue, and never blame the client.

sections.title: Keeping money and payment details safe

head: Risk
What to do
rows: Close the drawer after every sale. Lock the till or log out and take the key when you leave the desk, even for a few minutes.
Too much cash in the till
Take large amounts of cash out during a busy day, record it and put it in the safe, as the salon's policy says, so less is at risk in a robbery.
Count out of sight of clients.
Only staff allowed to use the till have the key or code. Never share it.
Robbery on the way to the bank
Take cash to the bank at different times and by different routes, as the owner plans, ideally with two people.
Never write down or keep card numbers or PINs; store card slips safely.
Keep receipts and records in a locked place.

blocks.note: In a robbery, do not resist. Hand over the money, stay calm, do what you are told and call the police on 119 afterwards. No amount of money is worth anyone's safety.
blocks.label: Safety

ul: Do not leave bags, cash or paperwork on the counter.
Count notes carefully and keep them tidy in the drawer, facing the same way.
Report anything that looks wrong: a missing key, a damaged drawer, a stranger watching the till.

blocks.p: **Petty cash** is a small amount of cash kept for everyday needs such as milk for clients' tea or cleaning cloths. Every payment from it gets a slip or receipt, and the total of slips plus cash left must equal the amount you started with.

sections.title: Cashing up at the end of the day

blocks.p: **Cashing up** (balancing the till) means counting the takings and checking them against the sales record. All the money a salon takes in sales in a day is its **takings**.

flow: After the last client has paid, print the till's end-of-day report (on many tills, the 'Z reading')
Take the drawer to a safe place away from clients, ideally with a second person
Take out the float for tomorrow, counted and bagged
Count the cash by value and write each amount on the cash-up sheet
Add up the card slips and check them against the card machine's total
Count the vouchers taken and check refunds and petty cash slips
Compare each total with the till report
Sign the cash-up sheet; prepare the deposit slip; store cash and records in the safe

blocks.h: How much should be in the drawer?

blocks.p: Cash that should be in the drawer = **float + cash sales** - any cash refunds or petty cash paid out.

head: Example
Working
rows: Till should hold J$62,000 but holds J$61,500
Three clients pay cash: J$4,500, J$2,750, J$6,000
A J$10,000 float with J$5,000 in J$1,000 notes; rest in J$500 notes

blocks.p: If the drawer has less than it should, the till is **short**; if more, it is **over**.

flow: Do not panic or hide the difference
Count again carefully and check your addition
Check receipts, card slips, vouchers, refunds and petty cash
Look for the common causes: a wrong price keyed in, a card payment keyed as cash, wrong change, an unrecorded refund or voucher
Record the amount and details on the cash-up sheet
Report it to the supervisor

blocks.note: Never make up a shortage from the tip jar or your own purse, and never change the sales record to match. Even a small difference can show a procedure problem, a till fault or theft. Honest reporting protects you and keeps the accounts correct.
blocks.label: Remember

ul: Fill in a **deposit slip** (also called a lodgement or paying-in slip) showing the cash to be banked. The bank stamps your copy as proof.
Bag the cash securely, take it at different times and routes as the owner plans, and keep the stamped slip with the records.
Keep the float aside; it is not banked.

sections.title: Service at the till and keeping records

ul: Greet each client with a smile and use her name.
If there is a queue, acknowledge the waiting clients and serve each one in turn. Never rush the checks.
Read the bill out clearly so the client can check each service and product, and explain any GCT, discount or deposit.
Offer the payment methods the salon accepts. Count change back carefully, give a receipt every time and keep card details private.
If a client questions the bill, listen, apologise and check it against the record; call the supervisor if you cannot solve it.
Do not give discounts or credit the policy does not allow; explain politely.

head: Record
What it shows
rows: The float counted at opening, signed.
Every sale, item, price and payment type.
Vouchers issued, used and their balances.
Deposits taken and the booking they hold.
The day's counts, differences and banking.

ul: Records must be **neat, correct and safe**: they are needed for the accounts and for tax.
Keep payment records and client details private. Do not photograph or share real names or card numbers.

blocks.note: Payment records are personal and business information. Keep them in a locked place or a password-protected system and let only authorised staff see them, as the data protection law requires.
blocks.label: Jamaica

ul: I can count a float with a witness, record it and report a shortage before sales.
I can check the till, card machine, receipt rolls and price list before opening.
I can work out a bill in J$, apply a discount, deposit or voucher, and add GCT at the rate I am given.
I can take a cash payment: say the amount, keep the note on the counter, count change back.
I can check a banknote by look, feel and tilt, and handle a note I think is forged without accusing the client.
I can take a chip-and-PIN or contactless payment so that the client keys in her own PIN.
I can handle a declined card quietly and politely.
I can handle mobile, transfer and split payments.
I can give a correct receipt for every sale.
I can accept a gift voucher or deposit and record it.
I can give only listed discounts and refer other requests to the manager.
I can follow the steps for a refund and record it with a supervisor's signature.
I can keep the drawer closed, lock the till when I leave, and take extra cash to the safe.
I can describe safe banking and what to do in a robbery.
I can cash up, calculate what should be in the drawer, and report a shortage or overage.
I can give polite service at the till and keep payment records neat, correct and private.

blocks.note: In essay answers, give the reason for each step. For example: 'I keep the client's note on the counter until she has her change, so there is no argument about which note she gave me.'
blocks.label: Tip

terms: Float
A set amount of change put in the till at the start of the day.
Takings
All the money a salon takes in sales in a day.
Till
The cash register or drawer where payments are recorded and kept.
Receipt
A record given to the client showing the date, items, prices, any GCT and the total.
GCT
General consumption tax, added to most goods and services at the current rate set by law.
Counterfeit
A fake banknote made to look real.
POS machine
Point of sale machine: the card machine.
PIN
Personal identification number for a bank card; keyed in only by the client.
Chip
The small square on a bank card that holds its data.
Contactless
Paying by tapping a card or phone on the machine.
Declined
A card payment that the machine will not approve.
Mobile wallet
An app or account on a phone that holds money and can be used to pay.
Split payment
A bill paid in two ways, such as part cash and part card.
Voucher
A paper or electronic token worth a set amount, accepted as payment.
Deposit
Part of the price paid in advance to hold a booking.
Refund
Money given back to a client, usually by the way she paid.
Cash-up
Counting the takings and checking them against the sales record.
Z reading
On many tills, the end-of-day report showing the day's total sales.
Shortage (short)
Less money in the till than the record says there should be.
Overage (over)
More money in the till than the record says there should be.
Deposit (bank) slip
The form filled in when cash is paid into the bank.
Petty cash
A small amount of cash kept for everyday buys, with a slip for each payment.
Bank of Jamaica
The bank that issues Jamaica's notes and coins.

c1.title: Opening the till in Half Way Tree
c1.text: It is 8:00 a.m. at a salon and spa in Half Way Tree. Cashier Natalie collects the J$12,000 float from the safe. She is alone because her supervisor has gone to the bank. She counts the money once and finds J$11,500 in the drawer. The card machine is not connected and there are no spare receipt rolls.

c2.title: A busy Saturday at the till in Mandeville
c2.text: Cashier Jerome is serving at a salon in Mandeville. Mrs Hyacinth Morgan's bill is J$6,800. She hands him J$10,000. Behind her three clients are waiting, one of them looking at her watch. Jerome has put Mrs Morgan's J$10,000 note into the drawer already. Mrs Morgan then says she gave him a J$5,000 note, not J$10,000.

c3.title: Vouchers, deposits and discounts in Negril
c3.text: At a spa in Negril, a client, Ms Andrea Dixon, presents a gift voucher worth J$8,000 for treatments that come to J$11,500. Another client, a bride, has booked a bridal day for J$24,000 and paid a 50% deposit two weeks ago. A friend of the receptionist asks for a 30% discount on a pedicure of J$4,000 that is not on the price list.

c4.title: A card that does not work in Spanish Town
c4.text: Mrs Pauline Edwards, a client in a Spanish Town salon, taps her card for a bill of J$7,350 and the machine shows 'DECLINED'. There are other clients standing close. She says she has money in her account. The cashier, Troy, offers to write down her card number and PIN so that he can enter them later.

c5.title: Cashing up in Ocho Rios
c5.text: At the end of the day at a salon in Ocho Rios the float was J$10,000 and cash sales on the till report are J$41,500. Cashier Marsha counts the drawer and finds J$49,700. She wants to take J$200 from the tip jar to 'make it right' or to adjust the sales record.

questions.q: What should Natalie do about the J$500 difference in the float?
o: Put J$500 of her own money in the drawer to make it right
Open for business and look into it at the end of the day
Report the shortage to her supervisor and record it before taking sales
Write the float on the sheet as J$12,000, since that is what the safe holds
questions.why: Count the float, record the amount and report any difference before sales begin. A difference found later cannot be traced, and adding your own money or falsifying the sheet hides the problem.

questions.q: Why would it have been better for Natalie to count the float with another person watching?
o: It makes the count go faster, as two people can sort the notes at once
A witness can confirm the amount, which protects the cashier and the salon
The salon's insurance only pays out when two people have signed the sheet
It keeps the supervisor informed about which notes are in the float
questions.why: A witness and a signed float sheet prove what was in the drawer at the start of the day. That protects an honest cashier from blame for a shortage that was not her fault.

questions.q: Why must a cashier never put her own money in the till?
o: A difference at cash-up could not be explained, and might look like theft
Coins from a bag can scratch the drawer and jam its sections
The insurance only covers notes that have come from clients
Her own notes would be taken to the bank with the takings by mistake
questions.why: The drawer must hold only the float and the day's takings, so any difference can be traced. Keep your bag and money in the staff area.

questions.q: How much change should Jerome give Mrs Morgan if she gave J$10,000 for a J$6,800 bill?
What went wrong in the way Jerome handled the note?
o: He counted the change back into her hand before closing the drawer
He said the amount out loud as he took the note from her
He checked the note's security features while she waited
He put her note into the drawer before giving her the change
questions.why: The client's note should stay on the counter until she has her change, so nobody can argue about which note was given. Saying the amount out loud also settles such arguments.

questions.q: Mrs Morgan now says she gave J$5,000. What is the best way for Jerome to settle it?
o: Apologise, call the supervisor, and check the till record and drawer
Agree with her and refund J$5,000 so that she goes away happy
Tell her she is mistaken and ask her to leave the counter at once
Pay the difference from the tip jar so the argument can end
questions.why: Stay polite and do not argue or pay from other money. Involve the supervisor, who can check the till record and the drawer. This is why you say the amount out loud and keep the note on the counter.

questions.q: Three clients are waiting while Jerome deals with Mrs Morgan. What should he do?
o: Rush Mrs Morgan, so that the others are not kept waiting any longer
Tell the waiting clients to come back later when it is quieter
Serve the next client while Mrs Morgan's problem is still open
Acknowledge them politely, then serve each in turn without rushing
questions.why: Good service means acknowledging waiting clients and serving each in turn. Rushing causes mistakes in money, and leaving a problem half-finished mixes up records.

questions.q: How much extra must Ms Dixon pay after her J$8,000 voucher on J$11,500 of treatments (before any other adjustment)?
questions.why: J$11,500 - J$8,000 = J$3,500. The voucher is marked as used and recorded.

questions.q: What must the cashier check first about Ms Dixon's voucher?
o: That it is the spa's own voucher, in date and not used before
That the colour is the right one for this season of the year
That Ms Dixon is the same person who first bought the voucher
That the treatments she chose cost more than the voucher's value
questions.why: A voucher must be genuine, in date and unused, checked against the voucher record. It is then marked as used so it cannot be used again.

questions.q: The bride paid a 50% deposit on the J$24,000 bridal day. How much does she pay on the day?
questions.why: 50% of J$24,000 is J$12,000, so the deposit was J$12,000 and J$24,000 - J$12,000 = J$12,000 remains.

questions.q: The receptionist's friend asks for a 30% discount that is not on the price list. What should the receptionist do?
o: Give it, since it only takes a small amount off the price of one pedicure
Give half of it and pay the rest of the difference from her own pocket
Refuse politely, and ask the manager or owner if it can be agreed
Give it, but record the sale at the full price in the sales book
questions.why: Only listed discounts may be given. Any other discount must be agreed by the manager or owner within the salon's policy. Recording a false price falsifies the records.

questions.q: The machine shows 'DECLINED'. What should Troy do first?
o: Say "You have no money in your account" so that she understands why
Tell her quietly that it was declined and ask for another way to pay
Try the card again and again until the machine finally approves it
Call the other clients over to witness that she cannot pay
questions.why: Tell the client quietly so that others cannot hear, without suggesting she has no money, then politely ask for another way to pay. One more try is allowed for a line fault, but repeated attempts are not.

questions.q: Troy offers to write down Mrs Edwards's card number and PIN. Why is this wrong?
o: It could be used for fraud and breaks her privacy
The salon's pen may not work on the receipt paper
The bank will charge the salon for each number written
She might change her PIN before he enters it
questions.why: Card numbers and PINs are never written down or kept. The client keys in her own PIN in private. Writing them down invites fraud and breaks her privacy.

questions.q: Mrs Edwards decides to pay J$2,000 in cash and the rest by another card that is approved. How much goes on the card?
questions.why: J$7,350 - J$2,000 = J$5,350. Take both payments and record each amount on the bill.

questions.q: How much cash should be in Marsha's drawer, given the float and the cash sales?
questions.why: Cash that should be in the drawer is the float plus cash sales: J$10,000 + J$41,500 = J$51,500.

questions.q: Marsha counted J$49,700. What is the position of the till?
o: Over by J$1,800
Short by J$800
Short by J$1,800
Balanced
questions.why: J$51,500 - J$49,700 = J$1,800 short. A till with less than the record says is short.

questions.q: What should Marsha do first about the difference?
o: Take J$1,800 from the tip jar to make up the drawer
Change the sales record down to J$39,700 so that it matches
Count again, check receipts, slips and refunds, then report it
Say nothing, since it was only a small amount of money
questions.why: Count again, look for the causes (wrong price, card keyed as cash, wrong change, unrecorded refund or voucher), then record and report. Never make it up from other money or change the record.

questions.q: A cashier wants to check a large note she thinks may be forged. Which is a sensible way to check?
o: Rub it hard to see if the ink comes off
Look, feel and tilt it to check its security features
Hold it up and tell the client loudly what she suspects
Put it in the till and check it at the end of the day
questions.why: Look at the print and colours, feel the paper and raised print, and tilt it to see features that change with the light. Stay polite, and call the supervisor if you think it is forged.

questions.q: During a robbery at the reception desk, what should the cashier do?
o: Hold on to the drawer and stay at the desk until the police arrive
Hand over the money, stay calm, and call the police on 119 afterwards
Follow the robber outside to see which way he goes, so she can tell the police
Press the till shut and refuse to open it, so that he cannot take the money
questions.why: No amount of money is worth anyone's safety. Do not resist, do what you are told, and call the police on 119 once it is safe.

questions.q: The petty cash tin started the week with J$3,000. Slips show J$450 spent on milk and J$800 on cleaning cloths. How much cash should be left in the tin?
questions.why: Slips plus cash left must equal the starting amount. J$450 + J$800 = J$1,250 spent, so J$3,000 - J$1,250 = J$1,750 left.
